title: Cost-Effectiveness and Implementation of Community Clinical Linkage Models to Increase Female Breast and Cervical Cancer Screening
content: Introduction: Community-clinical linkage models that integrate community health workers (CHWs) into cancer screening outreach offer an important strategy for addressing persistent disparities in preventive care. This study evaluates the cost-effectiveness and implementation experiences of two CCL programs in Colorado, one urban, one rural, that transitioned from a generalized outreach model, the Targeted Outreach Program (TOP), to an individualized model, the Community Outreach (TCO) program, whereby CHWs focused on reducing breast and cervical cancer screening barriers for hard-to-reach women. Methods: The Colorado Department of Public Health and the Environment provided data from the final year of TOP, 2018, and the first three years of TCO, 2019 -2021. We identified barriers to screening and types of direct assistance provided, and program costs. We assessed changes in screening rates, average cost per woman screened, and cost per additional woman screened during TCO implementation and between TOP and TCO. Results: The urban site screening rate initially fell with TCO, as outreach shifted from electronic health record identification to community outreach, while the rural rate remained constant. In TCO year two, the percent of Hispanic women served in the urban site increased, as did screening rates, at a cost of $3740 per additional woman screened. At the rural site, the cost per woman screened declined by $155, while the screening rate rose in TCO year two. The COVID-19 pandemic affected sites differently, with the rural site having limited capacity to adapt, leading to a 45 percentage point (pp) decline in the screening rate. When comparing TOP with the second year of TCO, to avoid the pandemic effect, the urban site screening rate was 4 pp lower, while the rural site rate was 28 pp lower, at a cost of $543 per additional woman screened. Conclusions: While the results underscore the promise of CHW-led outreach in promoting equitable access to breast and cervical cancer screening, cost-effectiveness varied over time as infrastructure, resources, and the populations served shaped screening outcomes and the cost trajectory of CCL models providing outreach cancer screening to underserved women in diverse geographic settings.
